title: Hospitals Dropping Medicare Advantage: What to Do

sections.text: Why Hospitals Are Dropping Medicare Advantage Plans

sections.content: Hospital systems in many states have ended or scaled back their contracts with Medicare Advantage insurers, citing payment disputes and delays caused by prior authorization requirements. If your hospital or health system sent you a letter about network changes for 2026, you are not alone, and the timing is not a coincidence.

These disputes typically center on how much and how quickly insurers reimburse hospitals, along with frustration over claim denials. The trend has touched large academic medical centers as well as smaller regional and rural hospitals, so plan size or hospital size does not guarantee protection from a contract termination.

sections.text: How This Trend Could Affect Your Coverage

sections.content: One confusing part of these network exits is timing. Your Medicare Advantage plan's provider directory may still list your hospital as in-network even after the contract has actually ended, because directories are not always updated the moment a change takes effect.

If you receive care at a hospital that has left your plan's network, the cost difference can be significant. Depending on your plan type, out-of-network care may come with much higher cost sharing, or in some cases no coverage at all outside of emergencies. For anyone managing an ongoing condition, a sudden network change can also disrupt care with a specialist or treatment team you have worked with for years.

sections.text: HMO vs. PPO: Does Your Plan Type Change the Risk?

sections.content: Your plan type changes how exposed you are to a network exit. HMO plans generally require you to use in-network providers except in emergencies, so losing your hospital can mean losing access to it entirely under that plan. PPO plans allow you to see out-of-network providers, but usually at a noticeably higher copay or coinsurance than staying in-network.

sections.text: How to Check if Your Hospital Is Leaving Your Plan's Network

sections.content: The most reliable first step is calling your hospital's billing or patient services department and asking directly whether they plan to renew their Medicare Advantage contracts for 2026. Hospital staff who handle insurance contracts usually know about terminations well before they are widely publicized.

You can also review your plan's online provider directory, though you should treat it as a starting point rather than the final word, since directories can lag behind actual contract changes. Watch your mail for official notices from either your insurer or your hospital system, since both are generally required to inform members ahead of a network change taking effect for the new plan year.

sections.text: What to Do If Your Doctors or Hospital Are Leaving Your Plan

sections.content: If you confirm your hospital is leaving your plan's network, start by comparing your current Medicare Advantage plan against other Medicare Advantage plans available in your area that still include that hospital. Plan networks vary by county and by insurer, so another plan may offer the same hospital access without requiring you to change providers.

It is also worth considering Original Medicare paired with a Medigap policy, since this combination generally allows you to see any provider that accepts Medicare, which can offer more consistent long-term access to hospitals and specialists. If you are weighing this option, review how a [Medicare Supplement plan](/medicare-supplement-plans/plan-g/) compares with your current Medicare Advantage costs and coverage.

Before switching anything, check how your prescription drug coverage would change. Formularies, the lists of covered drugs, vary between insurers, so a plan that solves your hospital access problem could still create a new issue if your medications are not covered the same way.

sections.text: When You Can Make a Plan Change

sections.content: For most coverage changes, you will need to wait for the Annual Enrollment Period, which runs from October 15 to December 7 each year, with changes taking effect January 1. In some cases, a Special Enrollment Period may be available if your plan significantly reduces its provider network outside of this window, which can allow you to switch plans before the next annual enrollment cycle.

sections.calloutText: If you miss the Annual Enrollment Period and do not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you may be locked into your current plan's network until the next enrollment cycle. Confirming your hospital's status early gives you more time to act within the correct window.

sections.text: Avoiding Costly Mistakes During a Network Change

sections.content: Do not assume a scheduled procedure, surgery, or ongoing treatment at your hospital will be covered the same way once a contract ends. Confirm network status with both your hospital and your insurer before the date of service, since coverage decisions are based on whether the contract is active at the time care is provided, not when you originally scheduled it.

Pay close attention to enrollment deadlines so you do not end up stuck in a plan that no longer includes the hospital or specialists you rely on. It is also worth keeping copies of any letters, emails, or notices from your hospital or insurer about the network change, since these records can be useful if a billing dispute comes up later.

Before you assume your plan still covers your hospital, call both your hospital's billing department and your insurer's member services line and ask the same question: is this hospital in-network as of January 1, 2026. Getting the answer from both sides helps you catch any mismatch between what the directory shows and what is actually true.

sections.text: Getting Help Without the Pressure of a Sales Pitch

sections.content: A licensed Medicare agent can walk through plan options with you based on your specific hospital, doctors, and prescriptions, rather than asking you to compare plans on your own from a generic list. A trustworthy comparison should center on your medical needs and budget, not steer you toward a particular insurer for reasons unrelated to your coverage.
You are allowed to take the time you need to review your options. Understanding your coverage fully before making a change matters more than acting quickly.

faqs.question: I just found out my hospital may be leaving my plan. Do I need to decide right away?
faqs.answer: No. While it helps to confirm the network status now, actual plan changes generally need to happen during the Annual Enrollment Period from October 15 to December 7, or during a qualifying Special Enrollment Period. You have time to research your options calmly before committing to a new plan.

faqs.question: Can I get information about my options without a pushy sales call?
faqs.answer: Yes. Licensed Medicare agents can provide plain-language comparisons of plans based on your hospital, doctors, and prescriptions without pressuring you to enroll immediately. Reputable sources will explain what plans are available in your area and let you decide when, or whether, to make a change.

faqs.question: How do I know if a source explaining Medicare Advantage changes is trustworthy?
faqs.answer: Look for clear transparency about licensing, which plans and carriers are available, and how recommendations are made. A trustworthy source explains coverage details and tradeoffs plainly, rather than using vague promises, exaggerated claims, or urgency-driven language to rush your decision.

faqs.question: What if I switch plans and still end up with the wrong coverage?
faqs.answer: Comparing plans based on your actual doctors, hospital, and prescription list significantly reduces this risk, since it grounds the comparison in your real medical needs rather than general features. If your needs or network access change again later, future enrollment periods allow you to adjust your coverage.

sections.text: Your Next Step: Confirm Your Hospital's Network Status Today

sections.content: Rather than waiting until the Annual Enrollment Period is nearly over, reach out to your hospital or a licensed Medicare agent now to confirm whether your hospital's contract with your plan is changing for 2026. Getting clear, current information early gives you room to compare options without rushing a decision under deadline pressure.

excerpt: Hospitals across the country are dropping Medicare Advantage contracts over payment disputes, leaving members at risk of losing in-network access in 2026.
keyTakeaways: Hospitals are ending Medicare Advantage contracts nationwide due to payment delays, low reimbursement, and claim denial disputes
Provider directories may not reflect contract terminations in real time, so confirm network status directly with your hospital
HMO members risk losing access entirely, while PPO members face higher out-of-network costs
Compare other Medicare Advantage plans in your area or consider Original Medicare plus Medigap for more consistent hospital access
Watch for official notices from your insurer or hospital system ahead of 2026 network changes
